orig_9709_p3_int_standard.description: Recognise the standard primitives, reverse a linear inside slope and evaluate exact definite integrals on the right interval.

sections.title: Why divide by the inner slope?
sections.label: Reverse a linear inner slope
sections.intro: Integration reverses differentiation. Take a known primitive of the outer function and check what differentiation would multiply it by.

blocks.html: If \(F'=f\) and \(a\ne0\), then \(\int f(ax+b)\,\mathrm dx=\frac1aF(ax+b)+C\), where the expressions are defined. Differentiating the right-hand side produces the factor \(a\), which cancels \(\frac1a\).

figure.alt: Two exponential curves rise to the right. The upper curve is twice the height of the lower curve at the same input.
figure.caption: The lower curve is \(\tfrac12\mathrm e^{2x}\). Its slope at the marked input equals the height of the upper curve \(\mathrm e^{2x}\) there.

blocks.html:
IntegrandPrimitive before adding \(C\)
\(e^{ax+b}\)\(\frac1a e^{ax+b}\)
\(\frac1{ax+b}\)\(\frac1a\ln|ax+b|\)
\(\sin(ax+b)\)\(-\frac1a\cos(ax+b)\)
\(\cos(ax+b)\)\(\frac1a\sin(ax+b)\)
\(\sec^2(ax+b)\)\(\frac1a\tan(ax+b)\)
\(\frac1{x^2+c^2}\), \(c>0\)\(\frac1c\arctan\left(\frac xc\right)\)
Use the signed value of \(a\). Division by its magnitude alone fails when the inside decreases.

blocks.title: Find the exponential coefficient

retry.feedback: Keep the sign of the inner slope. Dividing \(6\) by \(-2\) gives \(-3\).

blocks.hint: The signed slope of \(1-2x\) is \(-2\).
blocks.solution: Differentiate \(ke^{1-2x}\) to obtain \(-2ke^{1-2x}\). Thus \(-2k=6\), so \(k=-3\).

sections.title: When does the logarithm need a modulus?
sections.label: Use the original domain
sections.intro: A reciprocal linear function has one excluded input. On either interval where its denominator is non-zero, the modulus makes the logarithm defined.

blocks.html: On any interval with \(ax+b\ne0\), the derivative of \(\ln|ax+b|\) is \(\frac a{ax+b}\). For definite integrals use one continuous interval and evaluate the primitive at the upper limit minus its value at the lower limit.
Finite values at both endpoints are insufficient for the subtraction rule. A zero of the denominator between them interrupts the interval.

blocks.title: Read the ratio of endpoint magnitudes

retry.feedback: Subtract the lower primitive value from the upper value. The upper magnitude goes on top.

blocks.hint: The denominator is negative throughout. Use its absolute value at each endpoint, upper over lower.
blocks.solution: The primitive is \(\ln|4x-6|\) on the interval. Upper minus lower is \(\ln2-\ln6=\ln\left(\frac13\right)\).

sections.title: Where does the minus sign go with sine?
sections.label: Integrate sine and cosine in radians
sections.intro: Use \(\sin u\mapsto-\cos u\) and \(\cos u\mapsto\sin u\). Then divide by the slope of the angle; the standard trigonometric rules use radians.

blocks.html: With \(a\ne0\), the coefficient of the cosine primitive for \(\sin(ax+b)\) is \(-\frac1a\). The coefficient of the sine primitive for \(\cos(ax+b)\) is \(\frac1a\).
If an angle is expressed as a degree variable \(\theta\), replace the argument by \(\frac{\pi\theta}{180}\) in radians before using these formulas.

blocks.title: Match both trigonometric coefficients

retry.feedback: The primitive of sine has a minus sign.

blocks.hint: Differentiate each candidate term; check which gains a minus sign and which gains a positive multiplier.
blocks.solution:
\(-2A=5\) because the derivative of cosine is negative sine. \(4B=-3\) from differentiating sine.

So \(A=-\frac52\) and \(B=-\frac34\).

sections.title: Does the primitive use tangent or inverse tangent?
sections.label: Recognise the two different patterns
sections.intro: \(\sec^2(ax+b)\) calls for tangent. A positive quadratic of the form \(x^2+c^2\) in a reciprocal calls for inverse tangent.

blocks.html: \(\int\sec^2(ax+b)\,\mathrm dx=\frac1a\tan(ax+b)+C\). For \(c>0\), \(\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dx}\arctan\left(\frac xc\right)=\frac c{x^2+c^2}\), so divide by \(c\) for the reciprocal quadratic.
A \(\sec^2\) integrand is undefined where its cosine denominator is zero. A reciprocal \(x^2+c^2\) with \(c>0\) has no real pole.

blocks.title: Evaluate both exact integrals
blocks.hint: At each upper limit the tangent angle is \(\frac{\pi}{4}\), or the inverse tangent input is \(1\).
blocks.solution:
The first is \(\big[2\tan(2x)\big]_0^{\frac{\pi}{8}}=2\).

The second is \(\left[\frac32\arctan\left(\frac x2\right)\right]_0^2=\frac{3\pi}{8}\).

sections.title: How can I prove that the inner scale is right?
sections.label: Check by differentiating
sections.intro: The chain rule makes the candidate primitive testable.

blocks.html: Differentiate the proposed primitive. Check the returned denominator, its scale, and the sign against the original integrand.
An inverse tangent primitive is for a sum of squares, while a tangent primitive comes from squared secant.

blocks.title: Match a sum of squares to inverse tangent
blocks.hint: Factor the constant term in the denominator before matching inverse tangent.
blocks.solution:
Factor \(4\) out of the denominator to obtain the pattern \(\frac1{1+u^2}\).

Use \(u=\frac{3 x}{2}\). Taking the derivative of the inverse tangent introduces \(\frac{3}{2}\).

Comparing with the proposed primitive gives \(a=\frac{5}{6}\).

glossary.definition: A function whose derivative is the integrand.
An excluded input where these reciprocal functions grow without bound.

examples.title: Undo the inner exponential slope
examples.question: Find \(\int 6e^{2x-3}\,\mathrm dx\).
solution: Differentiating \(e^{2x-3}\) produces \(2e^{2x-3}\). The exponential keeps its whole exponent.
To get the coefficient \(6\), multiply the primitive by \(\frac62=3\).
The answer is \(3e^{2x-3}+C\), since its derivative is the original integrand.

examples.title: Use the logarithm on a negative branch
examples.question: Evaluate \(\int_{-2}^{-1}\frac3{3x+2}\,\mathrm dx\) as a single logarithm.
solution: The linear denominator is negative throughout this interval and has no zero there.
The integrand is the derivative of \(\ln|3x+2|\). The expression inside the modulus is evaluated at both limits.
Upper minus lower gives \(\ln 1-\ln 4=\ln\left(\frac14\right)\).

examples.title: Track both the inner slope and the sine sign
examples.question: Find \(\int\big(3\sin(2x+1)+4\cos(1-4x)\big)\,\mathrm dx\).
solution: For the sine term use negative cosine and divide by \(2\), giving \(-\frac32\cos(2x+1)\).
For the cosine term use sine and divide by the signed inner slope \(-4\), giving \(-\sin(1-4x)\).
Therefore the primitive is \(-\frac32\cos(2x+1)-\sin(1-4x)+C\). Differentiating checks both signs.

examples.title: Distinguish a tangent primitive from an inverse tangent
examples.question: Evaluate \(\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{12}}6\sec^2(3x)\,\mathrm dx\) and \(\int_0^3\frac6{x^2+9}\,\mathrm dx\).
solution: In the first integral the argument \(3x\) never reaches a pole. Use \(\big[2\tan(3x)\big]_0^{\frac{\pi}{12}}=2\).
For the second, \(x^2+9=x^2+3^2\). The primitive is \(2\arctan\left(\frac x3\right)\).
The second integral is \(2(\arctan1-\arctan0)=\frac{\pi}{2}\).

examples.title: Undo the slope of the exponent
examples.question: Find \(a\) if \(\int 9 \mathrm e^{3 - 2 x}\,\mathrm dx=a\left(\mathrm e^{3 - 2 x}\right)+C\).
solution: The derivative of the exponent is \(-2\).
Differentiating \(a\mathrm e^{3 - 2 x}\) introduces an extra factor \(-2\). Divide the original multiplier by it.
Comparing with the proposed primitive gives \(a=- \frac{9}{2}\).

examples.title: Choose the logarithm for the correct domain
examples.question: Find \(a\) if \(\int \frac{7}{3 x + 2}\,\mathrm dx=a\left(\ln{\left(- 3 x - 2 \right)}\right)+C\). Use \(x<- \frac{2}{3}\).
solution: The derivative of the denominator is \(3\). A logarithm of its absolute value differentiates to \(\frac{3}{3 x + 2}\).
Use \(\ln(- 3 x - 2)\) on the stated branch.
Comparing with the proposed primitive gives \(a=\frac{7}{3}\).

examples.title: Match a sum of squares to inverse tangent
examples.question: Find \(a\) if \(\int \frac{7}{4 x^{2} + 25}\,\mathrm dx=a\left(\operatorname{atan}{\left(\frac{2 x}{5} \right)}\right)+C\).
solution: Factor \(25\) out of the denominator to obtain the pattern \(\frac1{1+u^2}\).
Use \(u=\frac{2 x}{5}\). Taking the derivative of the inverse tangent introduces \(\frac{2}{5}\).
Comparing with the proposed primitive gives \(a=\frac{7}{10}\).

extraPractice.title: Undo the slope of the exponent
extraPractice.prompt: Find \(a\) if \(\int 7 \mathrm e^{5 x - 2}\,\mathrm dx=a\left(\mathrm e^{5 x - 2}\right)+C\).
extraPractice.hint: Reverse the chain rule by dividing by the inner derivative.
extraPractice.solution:
The derivative of the exponent is \(5\).

Differentiating \(a\mathrm e^{5 x - 2}\) introduces an extra factor \(5\). Divide the original multiplier by it.

Comparing with the proposed primitive gives \(a=\frac{7}{5}\).

extraPractice.title: Choose the logarithm for the correct domain
extraPractice.hint: Use the positive expression inside the logarithm on the given branch.
extraPractice.solution:
The derivative of the denominator is \(4\). A logarithm of its absolute value differentiates to \(\frac{4}{4 x + 5}\).

Use \(\ln(- 4 x - 5)\) on the stated branch.

Comparing with the proposed primitive gives \(a=\frac{3}{4}\).

extraPractice.title: Retain the inner angle and check the sign
extraPractice.hint: Differentiate the proposed cosine or sine primitive to confirm the sign and scale.
extraPractice.solution:
The inner derivative equals \(7\). Use the derivative of \(\cos{\left(7 x + \frac{\pi}{6} \right)}\) to see which sign is required.

Match the derivative of the proposed form to the original multiplier \(3\).

Comparing with the proposed primitive gives \(a=- \frac{3}{7}\).

extraPractice.title: Match a sum of squares to inverse tangent
extraPractice.hint: Factor the constant term in the denominator before matching inverse tangent.
extraPractice.solution:
Factor \(9\) out of the denominator to obtain the pattern \(\frac1{1+u^2}\).

Use \(u=\frac{4 x}{3}\). Taking the derivative of the inverse tangent introduces \(\frac{4}{3}\).

Comparing with the proposed primitive gives \(a=\frac{1}{6}\).

extraPractice.title: Retain the inner angle and check the sign
extraPractice.hint: Differentiate the proposed cosine or sine primitive to confirm the sign and scale.
extraPractice.solution:
The inner derivative equals \(-5\). Use the derivative of \(\cos{\left(5 x + \frac{\pi}{4} \right)}\) to see which sign is required.

Match the derivative of the proposed form to the original multiplier \(8\).

Comparing with the proposed primitive gives \(a=- \frac{8}{5}\).

extraPractice.title: Choose the logarithm for the correct domain
extraPractice.hint: Use the positive expression inside the logarithm on the given branch.
extraPractice.solution:
The derivative of the denominator is \(-3\). A logarithm of its absolute value differentiates to \(\frac{-3}{2 - 3 x}\).

Use \(\ln(2 - 3 x)\) on the stated branch.

Comparing with the proposed primitive gives \(a=-2\).

orig_9709_p3_int_trig_log.description: Rewrite trigonometric squares and products before integrating, and identify logarithmic derivatives and tangent integrals.

sections.title: How can a squared sine or cosine become a sum?
sections.label: Reduce a square using the double angle
sections.intro: Choose a double-angle identity that isolates the squared function. A constant term and an ordinary cosine are easier to integrate separately.

blocks.html: \(\cos(2u)=1-2\sin^2u=2\cos^2u-1\). Solve for the square before integrating.

figure.alt: A cosine-squared graph starts at one, drops to zero and returns to one each half-turn. A horizontal dashed line marks half height.
figure.caption: The dashed line is \(y=\tfrac12\). The graph of \(y=\cos^2x\) oscillates around it. This explains the constant term after using a double-angle identity.

blocks.html:
What you seeRewrite before integrating
\(\sin^2u\)\(\frac{1-\cos(2u)}2\)
\(\cos^2u\)\(\frac{1+\cos(2u)}2\)
\(\sin u\cos u\)\(\frac12\sin(2u)\)
\(\tan u\)\(\frac{\sin u}{\cos u}\), compare with the derivative of \(\cos u\)
Double the entire angle: if \(u=3x\), the cosine after rewriting is \(\cos(6x)\).

blocks.title: Integrate a squared sine
blocks.hint: Use the minus form for a sine square. The new angle is \(6x\).
blocks.solution:
\(4\sin^2(3x)=2-2\cos(6x)\).

The primitive \(2x-\frac13\sin(6x)\) gives \(\frac{\pi}{3}\) at the upper limit and \(0\) at the lower limit.

sections.title: What if sine and cosine share an angle?
sections.label: Replace the product with one sine
sections.intro: The identity for sine of a double angle turns an equal-angle product into a standard integral.

blocks.html: Use \(\sin u\cos u=\frac12\sin(2u)\), then apply the signed linear-argument rule.
Do not split a product into separate integrals. In this case the identity preserves the function and changes its shape.

blocks.title: Integrate a sine-cosine product

retry.feedback: The double-angle sine represents twice the product. Halve the coefficient before integrating.

blocks.hint: The product of the two functions equals half the sine of their doubled angle.
blocks.solution:
Rewrite the integrand as \(6\sin(4x)\).

Use \(\left[-\frac32\cos(4x)\right]_0^{\frac{\pi}{8}}=0+\frac32=\frac32\).

sections.title: When does a quotient lead to a logarithm?
sections.label: Match the derivative of the denominator
sections.intro: Keep the denominator as one function \(f\), differentiate it and compare the whole numerator with \(f'\). A constant mismatch can be taken outside.

blocks.html: On any interval where \(f\ne0\), \(\int k\frac{f'(x)}{f(x)}\,\mathrm dx=k\ln|f(x)|+C\). For continuous bounds, evaluate \(k\ln\left(\frac{|f(b)|}{|f(a)|}\right)\).
Matching just the highest power is insufficient. The whole numerator must equal one constant times \(f'\). Check for zeros of \(f\) between the bounds.

blocks.title: Match the multiplier and endpoint ratio
blocks.prompt: Write \(\int_0^2\frac{6x}{x^2+5}\,\mathrm dx=k\ln r\), with \(r=\frac{|f(2)|}{|f(0)|}\) and \(f(x)=x^2+5\). Give \(k\) and \(r\).

retry.feedback: Compare \(6x\) with \(2x\) to find the constant multiplier.

blocks.hint: The derivative of the denominator has coefficient two. Retain both endpoint values before taking their ratio.
blocks.solution:
The denominator derivative is \(2x\), so the multiplier is \(3\).

\(f(2)=9\), \(f(0)=5\), and the integral is \(3\ln\left(\frac95\right)\).

sections.title: Where does the minus sign come from when integrating tangent?
sections.label: Read tangent as a logarithmic derivative
sections.intro: Write tangent as sine divided by cosine. This exposes the negative sign in the derivative of cosine.

blocks.html: \(\int\tan x\,\mathrm dx=-\ln|\cos x|+C\). For \(a\ne0\), \(\int\tan(ax+b)\,\mathrm dx=-\frac1a\ln|\cos(ax+b)|+C\).
Keep the sign of a definite integral unless the question asks for an area. Check all intervening angles for zeros of cosine.

blocks.title: Evaluate tangent on a negative angle interval

retry.feedback: The integrand is negative before zero on this interval; the signed definite integral must be negative.

blocks.hint: Use \(-\ln|\cos x|\) and subtract its value at the lower limit.
blocks.solution:
At \(0\) the primitive is \(0\). At \(-\frac{\pi}{3}\) it is \(-\ln\left(\frac12\right)=\ln2\).

The difference is \(-\ln2\), so \(k=-1\).

sections.title: Why do I check the interval before using a trig logarithm?
sections.label: Check for poles
sections.intro: The logarithmic primitive of tangent is valid only on an interval with no pole.

blocks.html: Check that cosine cannot be zero between the bounds. Apply both endpoint values on the same connected interval.
A finite expression at both endpoints does not justify integrating across an undefined point.

blocks.title: Evaluate tangent on an interval with no pole
blocks.prompt: Write \(\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{8}}\tan(2x)\,\mathrm dx\) as \(a_0\ln r\), using the positive value of \(r\) obtained directly from the endpoint cosine ratio. Give \(a_0\) and \(r\).
blocks.hint: Treat the denominator as the inside of a logarithm and keep its negative derivative.
blocks.solution:
Rewrite tangent as \(\frac{\sin(ax)}{\cos(ax)}\). The derivative of its denominator is \(-a\sin(ax)\).

The primitive is \(- \frac{\ln{\left(\cos{\left(2 x \right)} \right)}}{2}\). Cosine stays positive on this interval.

Evaluate the logarithm at both ends. Because \(\cos 0=1\), the result is \(\frac{1}{2}\ln\left(\sqrt{2}\right)\).

glossary.definition: The argument \(2u\) built from the whole angle \(u\).
The net result once below-axis contributions have been subtracted.
An interval over which the expressions used in the calculation are defined and continuous.

examples.title: Replace a squared cosine with a doubled angle
examples.question: Evaluate \(\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}}6\cos^2(2x)\,\mathrm dx\).
solution: Use \(\cos^2u=\frac{1+\cos(2u)}2\) with \(u=2x\). The integrand becomes \(3+3\cos(4x)\).
A primitive is \(3x+\frac34\sin(4x)\). Its sine term is zero at both endpoints.
Upper minus lower gives \(\frac{3\pi}{4}\).

examples.title: Turn an equal-angle product into one sine
examples.question: Evaluate \(\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{6}}8\sin(3x)\cos(3x)\,\mathrm dx\).
solution: The double-angle identity gives \(8\sin(3x)\cos(3x)=4\sin(6x)\).
A primitive of \(4\sin(6x)\) is \(-\frac23\cos(6x)\).
Evaluate at the endpoints. The result is \(-\frac23\cos\pi+\frac23\cos0=\frac43\).

examples.title: Match a numerator to its denominator's derivative
examples.question: Evaluate \(\int_1^2\frac{9x^2}{x^3+5}\,\mathrm dx\), keeping the denominator intact.
solution: With \(f(x)=x^3+5\), its derivative is \(3x^2\). The numerator is \(3 f'(x)\).
The denominator is positive on the interval. A primitive is \(3\ln(x^3+5)\).
The value is \(3\ln13-3\ln6=3\ln\left(\frac{13}{6}\right)\).

examples.title: Integrate tangent from a logarithmic derivative
examples.question: Evaluate \(\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{3}}2\tan x\,\mathrm dx\).
solution: Write \(2\tan x=\frac{2\sin x}{\cos x}\). The derivative of \(\cos x\) is \(-\sin x\).
The integrand therefore has primitive \(-2\ln|\cos x|\). Cosine is positive and has no zero between the given limits.
The difference is \(-2\ln\left(\frac12\right)+2\ln1=2\ln2\).

examples.title: Separate the constant term from the doubled wave
examples.question: Write \(\int 7 \cos^{2}{\left(5 x \right)}\,\mathrm dx\) as \(Ax+B\sin(10x)+C\). Give \(A\) and \(B\).
solution: Use \(\cos^2 u=\frac{1+\cos 2u}{2}\) with \(u=5x\).
Integrating the constant term gives \(\frac{7}{2}x\). The cosine term contributes a sine with inner slope \(10\).
The primitive is \(\frac{7 x}{2} + \frac{7 \sin{\left(10 x \right)}}{20}+C\).

examples.title: Turn an equal-angle product into one sine
examples.question: Write \(\int 8 \sin{\left(3 x \right)} \cos{\left(3 x \right)}\,\mathrm dx\) as \(A\cos(6x)+C\). Find \(A\).
solution: Use \(2\sin u\cos u=\sin(2u)\) to rewrite the integrand.
The cosine primitive has negative sign and an extra factor from the inner slope. The final coefficient is \(- \frac{2}{3}\).

examples.title: Evaluate tangent on an interval with no pole
examples.question: Write \(\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{9}}\tan(3x)\,\mathrm dx\) as \(a_0\ln r\), using the positive value of \(r\) obtained directly from the endpoint cosine ratio. Give \(a_0\) and \(r\).
solution: Rewrite tangent as \(\frac{\sin(ax)}{\cos(ax)}\). The derivative of its denominator is \(-a\sin(ax)\).
The primitive is \(- \frac{\ln{\left(\cos{\left(3 x \right)} \right)}}{3}\). Cosine stays positive on this interval.
Evaluate the logarithm at both ends. Because \(\cos 0=1\), the result is \(\frac{1}{3}\ln\left(2\right)\).

Choose an identity

What you seeRewrite before integrating
\(\sin^2u\)\(\frac{1-\cos(2u)}2\)
\(\cos^2u\)\(\frac{1+\cos(2u)}2\)
\(\sin u\cos u\)\(\frac12\sin(2u)\)
\(\tan u\)\(\frac{\sin u}{\cos u}\), compare with the derivative of \(\cos u\)

Match a logarithmic derivative

When the numerator is \(k f'(x)\), the primitive of \(\frac{kf'(x)}{f(x)}\) is \(k\ln|f(x)|+C\) wherever \(f\ne0\).

Example: \(\int\tan(2x)\,\mathrm dx=-\frac12\ln|\cos(2x)|+C\), wherever it is defined.

• Double the whole angle.
  • Keep both the outside multiplier and the sign of the inner slope.
  • Locate any denominator zeros before evaluating a definite integral.
revision.examTip: Derive or write the identity before integrating. If the interval crosses a singularity, the ordinary endpoint subtraction does not apply.

extraPractice.title: Separate the constant term from the doubled wave
extraPractice.hint: Convert the square into a constant and one doubled-frequency cosine.
extraPractice.solution:
Use \(\sin^2u=\frac{1-\cos 2u}{2}\) with \(u=3x\).

Integrating the constant term gives \(\frac{5}{2}x\). The cosine term contributes a sine with inner slope \(6\).

The primitive is \(\frac{5 x}{2} - \frac{5 \sin{\left(6 x \right)}}{12}+C\).

extraPractice.title: Turn an equal-angle product into one sine
extraPractice.hint: Double the angle, then account separately for the one-half and the inner slope.
extraPractice.solution:
Use \(2\sin u\cos u=\sin(2u)\) to rewrite the integrand.

The cosine primitive has negative sign and an extra factor from the inner slope. The final coefficient is \(- \frac{3}{16}\).

extraPractice.title: Compare the whole numerator with the denominator derivative
extraPractice.prompt: Find \(a\) if \(\int \frac{16 x + 12}{2 x^{2} + 3 x + 5}\,\mathrm dx=a\left(\ln{\left(2 x^{2} + 3 x + 5 \right)}\right)+C\). Use \(x=1\text{ and nearby inputs}\).
extraPractice.hint: Compare the entire numerator with the derivative, including the constant term.
extraPractice.solution:
The derivative of the denominator is \(4 x + 3\).

Compare the entire numerator to it. Matching both terms gives the factor \(4\).

Comparing with the proposed primitive gives \(a=4\).

extraPractice.title: Evaluate tangent on an interval with no pole
extraPractice.prompt: Write \(\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{15}}\tan(5x)\,\mathrm dx\) as \(a_0\ln r\), using the positive value of \(r\) obtained directly from the endpoint cosine ratio. Give \(a_0\) and \(r\).
extraPractice.hint: Treat the denominator as the inside of a logarithm and keep its negative derivative.
extraPractice.solution:
Rewrite tangent as \(\frac{\sin(ax)}{\cos(ax)}\). The derivative of its denominator is \(-a\sin(ax)\).

The primitive is \(- \frac{\ln{\left(\cos{\left(5 x \right)} \right)}}{5}\). Cosine stays positive on this interval.

Evaluate the logarithm at both ends. Because \(\cos 0=1\), the result is \(\frac{1}{5}\ln\left(2\right)\).

extraPractice.title: Separate the constant term from the doubled wave
extraPractice.hint: Convert the square into a constant and one doubled-frequency cosine.
extraPractice.solution:
Use \(\cos^2 u=\frac{1+\cos 2u}{2}\) with \(u=7x\).

Integrating the constant term gives \(1x\). The cosine term contributes a sine with inner slope \(14\).

The primitive is \(x + \frac{\sin{\left(14 x \right)}}{14}+C\).

extraPractice.title: Turn an equal-angle product into one sine
extraPractice.hint: Double the angle, then account separately for the one-half and the inner slope.
extraPractice.solution:
Use \(2\sin u\cos u=\sin(2u)\) to rewrite the integrand.

The cosine primitive has negative sign and an extra factor from the inner slope. The final coefficient is \(- \frac{7}{20}\).

orig_9709_p3_int_partial_fractions.description: Decompose rational functions, integrate each part and check definite intervals for poles.

sections.title: How do separate linear factors produce logarithms?
sections.label: Distinct linear factors
sections.intro: First factor the denominator and check that the fraction is proper. Give each distinct linear factor a constant numerator. Clear the denominators to solve for the constants.

blocks.html: A term \(\frac{A}{ax+b}\) integrates to \(\frac Aa\ln|ax+b|+C\) when \(a\ne0\). The factor \(\frac1a\) compensates for the derivative of \(ax+b\).
After clearing denominators, substituting a root switches off every term except the one for that factor. This uses a polynomial identity, even though the original fraction is undefined at that root.

blocks.title: Find both logarithm coefficients
blocks.hint: Clear denominators and substitute both roots into the numerator identity.
blocks.solution: From \(7x+17=a(x+5)+b(x+2)\), the roots \(x=-2\) and \(x=-5\) give \(a=1,\ b=6\). Each linear factor has derivative one.

sections.title: What changes when a factor is squared?
sections.label: Keep the repeated powers
sections.intro: Include one term for each power of the repeated factor. For a squared linear factor that means keeping both the first power and the square.

blocks.html: A term with denominator \(ax+b\) gives a logarithm. A term \(\frac D{(ax+b)^2}\) gives \(-\frac D{a(ax+b)}\) because the exponent is \(-2\).
Omitting the first-power term at a repeated factor leaves too few coefficients to represent a general numerator. A reciprocal squared integrates by the power rule, with a minus sign.

blocks.title: Read the squared-factor coefficient and integrate it
blocks.prompt: The fraction \(\frac{7x+22}{(x+2)(x+4)^2}\) splits as \(\frac A{x+2}+\frac B{x+4}+\frac D{(x+4)^2}\). Give \(D\) and the coefficient \(k\) of \(\frac1{x+4}\) in its antiderivative.

retry.feedback: Integrating the power −2 introduces a minus sign.

blocks.hint: Clear the denominator and substitute \(x=-4\). Then integrate the squared-factor term.
blocks.solution: At \(x=-4\) the numerator is \(-6\) and the surviving term is \(-2D\), giving \(D=3\). The antiderivative contains \(-\frac3{x+4}\) so \(k=-3\).

sections.title: Why can one quadratic factor give two types of integral?
sections.label: Separate logarithm and inverse tangent
sections.intro: A real factor \(x^2+a^2\) with \(a>0\) does not split into real linear factors. Keep a numerator of degree at most one for that denominator.

blocks.html:
Term over \(x^2+a^2\)Matching antiderivative term
\(\frac{Bx}{x^2+a^2}\)\(\frac B2\ln(x^2+a^2)\)
\(\frac{D}{x^2+a^2}\)\(\frac Da\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac xa\right)\)
For a denominator \(cx^2+d\) of this kind, factor out \(c\) before reading the value of \(a\).

blocks.title: Find the three antiderivative coefficients
blocks.hint: First obtain the numerator over \(x^2+9\). Its derivative-matching term and constant integrate differently.
blocks.solution: The fraction splits as \(\frac1{x+1}+\frac{4x+2}{x^2+9}\). The logarithm of \(x^2+9\) has coefficient \(2\), and the inverse tangent has coefficient \(\frac23\).

sections.title: When do I divide first, and can I use the given limits?
sections.label: Divide and check the interval
sections.intro: If numerator and denominator have equal degree, divide to get a constant plus a proper fraction. Then decompose the proper remainder. Check the original denominator throughout any definite interval. Polynomial division also gives a proper remainder when the numerator degree is higher. Paper 3 partial-fraction cases go up to equal degrees.

blocks.html: For equal degrees subtract the denominator times the ratio of the leading coefficients. Integrate that constant as a multiple of \(x\) before adding the antiderivatives of the remaining fractions.

figure.alt: Two branches of a reciprocal graph approach opposite sides of a vertical dashed asymptote at x equals one. The highlighted test interval spans the pole.
figure.caption: The test interval shown crosses the pole at \(x=1\). The ordinary definite-integral method applies on a connected interval where the integrand is defined.

blocks.html: A pole inside the interval or at a limit prevents use of an ordinary definite integral across it. Finite values obtained by plugging the endpoints into an antiderivative do not fix the break.

blocks.title: Find the quotient and choose a valid interval
blocks.prompt: For \(R(x)=\frac{3x^2-4x-13}{(x-2)(x+1)}\), write \(R(x)=q+\frac A{x-2}+\frac B{x+1}\). Give \(q,A,B\) and choose the interval on which the ordinary definite integral is defined.

retry.feedback: The interval from zero to three contains the pole at two.

blocks.hint: Subtract three times the denominator. To choose the interval, test both roots of the denominator.
blocks.solution: Division leaves remainder \(-x-7\), which gives \(A=-3,\ B=2\). The poles are \(x=2\) and \(x=-1\). Only \([3,4]\) avoids both.

sections.title: How do I decide which part gives a logarithm?
sections.label: Identify the numerator pieces
sections.intro: A quadratic denominator often gives two different antiderivatives.

blocks.html: Separate the part proportional to the denominator derivative from the remaining constant.
A complete linear numerator usually needs both patterns, with a different scaling factor for each.

blocks.title: Match two numerator pieces with two different primitives
blocks.hint: Only the part proportional to the denominator derivative gives a logarithm.
blocks.solution:
Split the numerator into its \(x\) term and its constant.

The derivative of \(x^{2} + 4\) is \(2x\), so the logarithm coefficient is \(\frac{5}{2}\).

The constant part matches inverse tangent with an inner derivative factor. The second coefficient is \(\frac{3}{2}\).

glossary.definition: A rational fraction whose numerator has lower degree than its denominator.
A quadratic that cannot be factored into real linear factors.
A point where the rational expression grows without bound as its denominator approaches zero.

examples.title: Two different linear factors
examples.question: Integrate \(\frac{5x+7}{(x+1)(x+3)}\) with respect to \(x\).
solution: Clear denominators to obtain \(5x+7=A(x+3)+B(x+1)\).
At \(x=-1\) obtain \(A=1\). At \(x=-3\) obtain \(B=4\).
Integrate the two terms to get \(\ln|x+1|+4\ln|x+3|+C\). This holds on each interval without poles.

examples.title: Keep both powers of a repeated factor
examples.question: Integrate \(\frac{5x+11}{(x+1)(x+2)^2}\) with respect to \(x\).
solution: Use the form \(\frac A{x+1}+\frac B{x+2}+\frac D{(x+2)^2}\). Clearing denominators gives \(5x+11=A(x+2)^2+B(x+1)(x+2)+D(x+1)\).
Substitute \(x=-1\) and \(x=-2\) to get \(A=6\) and \(D=-1\). The coefficient of \(x^2\) gives \(A+B=0\), so \(B=-6\).
Integrate to get \(6\ln|x+1|-6\ln|x+2|+\frac1{x+2}+C\). The reciprocal term is positive because differentiating it gives the negative squared-denominator term.

examples.title: Split the numerator over a quadratic
examples.question: Integrate \(\frac{5x^2+7x+10}{(x+2)(x^2+4)}\) with respect to \(x\).
solution: Use \(\frac A{x+2}+\frac{Bx+D}{x^2+4}\). At \(x=-2\) the numerator identity gives \(A=2\). Comparing the quadratic and linear coefficients gives \(B=3\) and \(D=1\).
The numerator \(3x+1\) splits as \(\frac32(2x)+1\). The first part is a multiple of the derivative of \(x^2+4\).
Integrate to obtain \(2\ln|x+2|+\frac32\ln(x^2+4)+\frac12\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac x2\right)+C\).

examples.title: Divide before integrating a definite rational function
examples.question: Evaluate \(\int_2^4\frac{2x^2+7x-3}{(x-1)(x+2)}\,\mathrm dx\) exactly.
solution: The denominator is \(x^2+x-2\). Subtract twice this denominator from the numerator to get \(5x+1\).
The remainder splits as \(\frac{5x+1}{(x-1)(x+2)}=\frac2{x-1}+\frac3{x+2}\). Both poles lie outside the integration interval.
Use \(\left[2x+2\ln(x-1)+3\ln(x+2)\right]_2^4\). The exact value is \(4+2\ln3+3\ln\left(\frac32\right)\).

examples.title: Recover both coefficients before integration
examples.question: Write \(\frac{x + 10}{\left(x + 1\right) \left(x + 4\right)}\) as \(\frac{A}{x + 1}+\frac{B}{x + 4}\). Give \(A\) and \(B\).
solution: Each distinct linear factor gets its own numerator. Clear denominators with the original factorisation.
Matching coefficients gives \(A=3,\quad B=-2\).
For \(x>-1\), integrating term by term then gives \(3 \ln{\left(x + 1 \right)} - 2 \ln{\left(x + 4 \right)}+C\).

examples.title: Recover both coefficients before integration
examples.question: Write \(\frac{4 x + 17}{\left(x + 3\right)^{2}}\) as \(\frac{A}{x + 3}+\frac{B}{\left(x + 3\right)^{2}}\). Give \(A\) and \(B\).
solution: Each power of the repeated factor gets its own numerator. Clear denominators with the original factorisation.
Matching coefficients gives \(A=4,\quad B=5\).
For \(x>-3\), integrating term by term then gives \(4 \ln{\left(x + 3 \right)} - \frac{5}{x + 3}+C\).

examples.title: Match two numerator pieces with two different primitives
examples.question: Write \(\int \frac{8 x + 7}{x^{2} + 9}\,\mathrm dx\) as \(A\ln(x^{2} + 9)+B\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{x}{3}\right)+C\). Find \(A\) and \(B\).
solution: Split the numerator into its \(x\) term and its constant.
The derivative of \(x^{2} + 9\) is \(2x\), so the logarithm coefficient is \(4\).
The constant part matches inverse tangent with an inner derivative factor. The second coefficient is \(\frac{7}{3}\).

Start with a proper fraction

If the degrees are equal, subtract the constant quotient times the denominator. Decompose the remainder.

Match each term to its integral

\(\frac{A}{ax+b}\)\(\frac Aa\ln|ax+b|\)
\(\frac D{(ax+b)^2}\)\(-\frac{D}{a(ax+b)}\)
\(\frac{Bx+D}{x^2+a^2}\)\(\frac B2\ln(x^2+a^2)+\frac Da\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac xa\right)\)

One example

\(\frac{5x+7}{(x+1)(x+3)}=\frac1{x+1}+\frac4{x+3}\) gives \(\ln|x+1|+4\ln|x+3|+C\).

• Include every power of a repeated factor.
  • Check the chain multiplier on a logarithm.
  • Check both limits and the interval for poles.
revision.examTip: Use absolute values in logarithms of signed linear factors. An antiderivative is valid on each interval where the original function is defined.

orig_9709_p3_int_substitution.description: Use a given substitution to rewrite the integrand, transform limits and evaluate exact integrals.

sections.title: What must change when I use a given substitution?
sections.label: Replace the inner expression and differential
sections.intro: Write down the given substitution and differentiate it. Then group the original differential with the factor it needs. The transformed integral should have one variable.

blocks.html: For \(u=g(x)\), use \(\mathrm du=g'(x)\,\mathrm dx\). If your integrand has \(k g'(x)\,\mathrm dx\), carry the constant \(k\) into the new integral.
For an indefinite integral, restore the original variable in the final answer and include a constant of integration.

blocks.title: Find the factor and the exponent
blocks.prompt: Use \(u=5+x^2\) to evaluate \(\int4x(5+x^2)^2\,\mathrm dx\). Give \(a,n\) in the form \(a(5+x^2)^n+C\).
blocks.hint: The differential is \(\mathrm du=2x\,\mathrm dx\). Carry the remaining factor into the new integral.
blocks.solution: The integral is \(2\int u^2\,\mathrm du=\frac23u^3+C\). Restore the substitution to get \(a=\frac23\) and \(n=3\).

sections.title: What if an x is still left after substitution?
sections.label: Rewrite leftover factors
sections.intro: Sometimes the substitution replaces a square root but leaves a separate factor of \(x\). Rearrange the given relation to express that factor in terms of \(u\).

blocks.html: With \(u=\sqrt{ax+b}\), rewrite the relation as \(u^2=ax+b\) on its domain. Then \(x=\frac{u^2-b}{a}\) and \(\mathrm dx=\frac{2u}{a}\,\mathrm du\), for \(a\ne0\).
Writing \(\int f(x,u)\,\mathrm du\) with an unreplaced \(x\) leaves the change of variables incomplete.

blocks.title: Rewrite x and the differential together
blocks.hint: Use \(x=u^2-2\) and \(\mathrm dx=2u\,\mathrm du\) before cancelling the root.
blocks.solution: The integral transforms to \(2\int(u^2-2)\,\mathrm du=\frac23u^3-4u+C\). So \(a=\frac23,\ b=-4\).

sections.title: What happens when the substitution reverses the order of the limits?
sections.label: Transform definite limits in order
sections.intro: Apply the given substitution to the starting and finishing endpoints separately. If the substitution decreases, the new starting value can be larger than the finishing value.

blocks.html:
Original limitNew limit
\(x=a\)\(u=g(a)\)
\(x=b\)\(u=g(b)\)

Keep those limits in their original order or swap them and introduce a minus sign. Carry the factor from \(\mathrm dx\) as well.

figure.alt: A line falls as x increases. The first input x equals one maps to seven and the second input x equals three maps to three.
figure.caption: For \(u=9-2x\), inputs \(x=1\) then \(x=3\) give limits \(u=7\) then \(u=3\). The substitution also introduces a negative differential.

blocks.html: Sorting the new limits without changing the sign changes the value of the definite integral. Evaluating a formula in \(u\) at the old \(x\) limits also gives a different integral.

blocks.title: Transform both limits and evaluate
blocks.prompt: Use \(u=20-2x\) to evaluate \(\int_2^8\sqrt{20-2x}\,\mathrm dx\). Give the starting and finishing \(u\) limits in that order, then the exact value.
blocks.hint: Use the given order first. The differential contributes the factor \(-\frac12\).
blocks.solution: The limits are \(16\) and \(4\). The integral is \(-\frac12\int_{16}^4 u^{\frac12}\,\mathrm du=\frac13(64-8)=\frac{56}3\).

sections.title: How do I transform a trigonometric product completely?
sections.label: Use an identity for what remains
sections.intro: With \(u=\sin x\), one cosine factor belongs to the differential. The identity \(\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1\) converts an extra even power of cosine into a power of \(1-u^2\).

blocks.html: Write \(\cos^{2k+1}x=(\cos^2x)^k\cos x\). Then replace \(\cos^2x\) by \(1-u^2\) and \(\cos x\,\mathrm dx\) by \(\mathrm du\).
For \(u=\cos x\) the analogous substitution uses \(\mathrm du=-\sin x\,\mathrm dx\). Keep that sign and the transformed limits separate until you decide whether to swap the order.

blocks.title: Use the given trigonometric substitution
blocks.hint: Use one cosine in the differential and turn the remaining square into \(1-u^2\).
blocks.solution: The transformed integral is \(\int_0^1(u^3-u^5)\,\mathrm du=\frac14-\frac16=\frac1{12}\).

sections.title: How do the two negatives cancel in a decreasing substitution?
sections.label: Match bounds and differential
sections.intro: An increasing original variable can correspond to a decreasing new variable.

blocks.html: Leave transformed limits in their original order and retain the negative differential, or reverse the limits and change the sign once.
Two sign changes occur when both the reversed limits and the negative differential are changed. Account for each explicitly.

blocks.title: Keep the order when limits reverse
blocks.prompt: Use \(u=20 - 4 x\) to evaluate \(\int_{1}^{4}100 - 20 x\,\mathrm dx\). Give the transformed lower and upper limits in the original order, then the exact integral.
blocks.hint: Transform each endpoint in place and keep the sign from the differential.
blocks.solution:
At the original endpoints the new limits are \(16\) then \(4\).

\(\mathrm dx=-\frac{1}{4}\,\mathrm du\) contributes the minus sign. Swapping the transformed limits cancels it.

Evaluate the resulting positive integral to get \(150\).

glossary.definition: Replacing the variable of integration with a related one.
The piece such as dx or du that records the variable used in the integral.
The values of the new variable at the original starting and finishing endpoints.

examples.title: Change variables in an indefinite integral
examples.question: Evaluate \(\int 3x(1+x^2)^4\,\mathrm dx\) using \(u=1+x^2\).
solution: Differentiate \(u=1+x^2\) to get \(\mathrm du=2x\,\mathrm dx\). Hence \(3x\,\mathrm dx=\frac32\,\mathrm du\).
The integral becomes \(\frac32\int u^4\,\mathrm du=\frac3{10}u^5+C\).
Restore \(u=1+x^2\) to obtain \(\frac3{10}(1+x^2)^5+C\).

examples.title: Rewrite a leftover factor of x
examples.question: For \(x>-\frac12\), integrate \(\frac{x}{\sqrt{2x+1}}\) using \(u=\sqrt{2x+1}\).
solution: From \(u^2=2x+1\) obtain \(x=\frac{u^2-1}{2}\) and \(\mathrm dx=u\,\mathrm du\). In this domain \(u>0\).
The root in the denominator becomes \(u\). Therefore the integral is \(\frac12\int(u^2-1)\,\mathrm du\).
Integrate to get \(\frac16u^3-\frac12u+C\) then replace \(u\) to obtain \(\frac16(2x+1)^{\frac32}-\frac12(2x+1)^{\frac12}+C\).

examples.title: Respect decreasing limits
examples.question: Evaluate \(\int_0^4\sqrt{9-2x}\,\mathrm dx\) using \(u=9-2x\).
solution: The limits in order are \(x=0\mapsto u=9\) and \(x=4\mapsto u=1\). Also \(\mathrm dx=-\frac12\,\mathrm du\).
The integral is \(-\frac12\int_9^1 u^{\frac12}\,\mathrm du=\frac12\int_1^9u^{\frac12}\,\mathrm du\).
Evaluate \(\left[\frac13u^{\frac32}\right]_1^9=\frac13(27-1)=\frac{26}3\).

examples.title: Transform the whole trigonometric product
examples.question: Evaluate \(\int_0^{\frac\pi2}\sin^2x\cos^3x\,\mathrm dx\) using \(u=\sin x\).
solution: Set aside one \(\cos x\) for \(\mathrm du=\cos x\,\mathrm dx\). Rewrite the remaining \(\cos^2x\) as \(1-u^2\).
The limits \(0\) and \(\frac\pi2\) become \(0\) and \(1\). The integral becomes \(\int_0^1(u^2-u^4)\,\mathrm du\).
Evaluate \(\left[\frac{u^3}3-\frac{u^5}5\right]_0^1=\frac13-\frac15=\frac2{15}\).

examples.title: Rewrite a leftover linear factor
examples.question: Use \(u=3 x + 5\) in \(\int \left(3 x + 1\right) \left(3 x + 5\right)^{2}\,\mathrm dx\). In the resulting integral of \(Au^{3}+Bu^{2}\), give \(A\) and \(B\).
solution: The leftover factor is \(3 x + 1=u-4\). Also \(\mathrm dx=\frac{1}{3}\,\mathrm du\).
Multiplying gives \(u^{2} \left(\frac{u}{3} - \frac{4}{3}\right)\). This determines both requested coefficients.
Integrating in \(u\) gives \(\frac{u^{4}}{12} - \frac{4 u^{3}}{9}+C\). Substitute back to return to the original variable.

examples.title: Keep the order when limits reverse
examples.question: Use \(u=16 - 2 x\) to evaluate \(\int_{0}^{6}3 \sqrt{16 - 2 x}\,\mathrm dx\). Give the transformed lower and upper limits in the original order, then the exact integral.
solution: At the original endpoints the new limits are \(16\) then \(4\).
\(\mathrm dx=-\frac{1}{2}\,\mathrm du\) contributes the minus sign. Swapping the transformed limits cancels it.
Evaluate the resulting positive integral to get \(56\).

examples.title: Keep the order when limits reverse
examples.question: Use \(u=18 - 3 x\) to evaluate \(\int_{2}^{5}2 \sqrt{18 - 3 x}\,\mathrm dx\). Give the transformed lower and upper limits in the original order, then the exact integral.
solution: At the original endpoints the new limits are \(12\) then \(3\).
\(\mathrm dx=-\frac{1}{3}\,\mathrm du\) contributes the minus sign. Swapping the transformed limits cancels it.
Evaluate the resulting positive integral to get \(\frac{28 \sqrt{3}}{3}\).

revision.body:
Replace every part of the integral

For \(u=g(x)\), write \(\mathrm du=g'(x)\,\mathrm dx\). Rewrite any remaining \(x\) factors in terms of \(u\).

Finish in the right variable

Integral typeHow to finish
IndefiniteRestore the original variable and add \(C\).
DefiniteUse the transformed limits in their given order, or restore the original variable and keep the original limits.

One example

\(\int_0^4\sqrt{9-2x}\,\mathrm dx\) becomes \(-\frac12\int_9^1u^{\frac12}\,\mathrm du\) with \(u=9-2x\). Swap the limits to find \(\frac13(27-1)=\frac{26}3\).
revision.checks:
• Form the new differential with its sign and scale.
  • Rewrite the entire integrand in one variable.
  • Use endpoint values for the variable in the antiderivative.
revision.examTip: With \(u=\sin x\), keep one \(\cos x\) for the differential and replace each extra \(\cos^2x\) by \(1-u^2\).

extraPractice.title: Rewrite a leftover linear factor
extraPractice.prompt: Use \(u=4 x + 1\) in \(\int \left(4 x - 1\right) \left(4 x + 1\right)^{3}\,\mathrm dx\). In the resulting integral of \(Au^{4}+Bu^{3}\), give \(A\) and \(B\).
extraPractice.hint: Replace both the inside expression and the leftover factor before integrating.

The leftover factor is \(4 x - 1=u-2\). Also \(\mathrm dx=\frac{1}{4}\,\mathrm du\).

Multiplying gives \(u^{3} \left(\frac{u}{4} - \frac{1}{2}\right)\). This determines both requested coefficients.

Integrating in \(u\) gives \(\frac{u^{5}}{20} - \frac{u^{4}}{8}+C\). Substitute back to return to the original variable.

extraPractice.hint: Transform each endpoint in place and keep the sign from the differential.
extraPractice.solution:
At the original endpoints the new limits are \(26\) then \(6\).

\(\mathrm dx=-\frac{1}{5}\,\mathrm du\) contributes the minus sign. Swapping the transformed limits cancels it.

Evaluate the resulting positive integral to get \(192\).

extraPractice.hint: Replace both the inside expression and the leftover factor before integrating.

extraPractice.hint: Transform each endpoint in place and keep the sign from the differential.
extraPractice.solution:
At the original endpoints the new limits are \(25\) then \(4\).

\(\mathrm dx=-\frac{1}{3}\,\mathrm du\) contributes the minus sign. Swapping the transformed limits cancels it.

Evaluate the resulting positive integral to get \(52\).

extraPractice.title: Rewrite a leftover linear factor
extraPractice.prompt: Use \(u=2 x + 4\) in \(\int \left(2 x + 1\right) \left(2 x + 4\right)^{4}\,\mathrm dx\). In the resulting integral of \(Au^{5}+Bu^{4}\), give \(A\) and \(B\).
extraPractice.hint: Replace both the inside expression and the leftover factor before integrating.
extraPractice.solution:
The leftover factor is \(2 x + 1=u-3\). Also \(\mathrm dx=\frac{1}{2}\,\mathrm du\).

Multiplying gives \(u^{4} \left(\frac{u}{2} - \frac{3}{2}\right)\). This determines both requested coefficients.

Integrating in \(u\) gives \(\frac{u^{6}}{12} - \frac{3 u^{5}}{10}+C\). Substitute back to return to the original variable.

extraPractice.prompt: Use \(u=31 - 6 x\) to evaluate \(\int_{2}^{5}2 \left(31 - 6 x\right)^{2}\,\mathrm dx\). Give the transformed lower and upper limits in the original order, then the exact integral.
extraPractice.hint: Transform each endpoint in place and keep the sign from the differential.
extraPractice.solution:
At the original endpoints the new limits are \(19\) then \(1\).

\(\mathrm dx=-\frac{1}{6}\,\mathrm du\) contributes the minus sign. Swapping the transformed limits cancels it.

Evaluate the resulting positive integral to get \(762\).

orig_9709_p3_int_parts.description: Choose factors for integration by parts, simplify logarithmic and repeated products, and evaluate exact definite integrals.

sections.title: What makes a good choice of u?
sections.label: Choose the factors
sections.intro: Parts reverses the product rule. Arrange the two factors so that the second integral takes less work than the first.

blocks.html:
Write the integrand as \(uv'\). From \((uv)'=u'v+uv'\),

\[\int uv'\,dx=uv-\int u'v\,dx.\]

Choose \(u\) so its derivative is simpler, and choose \(v'\) so you know a primitive \(v\). First look for an inner function with its derivative, since that can make the reverse chain rule shorter.
The factor that appears in the integrand is \(v'\). Integrate it once before forming \(uv\).

blocks.title: Find the complete linear factor

retry.feedback: The remaining integral contributes another \(-3e^{-x}\). Include it in the constant coefficient.

blocks.hint: With \(v'=e^{-x}\), take \(v=-e^{-x}\). Keep the minus sign outside the remaining integral.

sections.title: How can I integrate a logarithm on its own?
sections.label: Use a factor of one
sections.intro: Write an isolated logarithm as \(1\times\) the logarithm. Its derivative is rational, so the next integral may admit an algebraic simplification.

blocks.html: For a positive argument, choose \(u=\ln g(x)\) when \(g'(x)\) divided by \(g(x)\) is simpler. With \(v'=1\), take \(v=x\). For \(\int x^n\ln x\,dx\), let \(v'\) be \(x^n\). The same idea works for inverse tangent, whose derivative is rational.
For \(\ln(3x+1)\), the real domain is \(3x+1>0\). Retain it even if the final expression can be written in several ways.

blocks.title: Find the coefficients of a log primitive
blocks.prompt: For \(x>0\), write \(\int x\ln x\,dx\) as \(A x^2\ln x+B x^2+C\). Give \(A\) and \(B\).

retry.feedback: The second integral is subtracted in integration by parts.

blocks.hint: Differentiate \(\ln x\) and integrate the other factor \(x\).
blocks.solution: Take \(u=\ln x,\ v=\frac{x^2}{2}\). The remainder is \(\int\frac{x}{2}\,dx=\frac{x^2}{4}\). Thus \(A=\frac12,\ B=-\frac14\).

sections.title: When should I use parts a second time?
sections.label: Repeat as the degree drops
sections.intro: A polynomial of degree two becomes linear after one use of parts. A second use removes the remaining variable factor.

blocks.html: Keep a new \(u,v'\) choice for each integral. If the other factor is exponential or sinusoidal, its primitive stays in a familiar family. Check both the sign of the outer remainder and the sign introduced by the next primitive.
An intermediate minus sign can multiply an entire new bracket. Write the second integral separately before recombining.

blocks.title: Recover a quadratic, linear and constant coefficient

retry.feedback: Subtract the constant contribution from the primitive of \((2x+4)e^x\).

blocks.hint: After the first step, write the primitive of \((2x+4)e^x\) in a separate line.
blocks.solution: Parts gives \((x^2+4x)e^x-\int(2x+4)e^x\,dx\). The latter primitive is \((2x+2)e^x\). Therefore \(A=1,\ B=2,\ D=-2\).

sections.title: How do I handle limits and signs?
sections.label: Use definite bounds
sections.intro: For an integral with bounds, apply both limits to the boundary term and keep the same limits on the remaining integral.

blocks.html:
Use \(\int_a^b uv'\,dx=[uv]_a^b-\int_a^b u'v\,dx\). Evaluate the upper endpoint first. A definite integral is signed. If the problem asks for geometric area, locate every crossing and add the magnitudes of the separate regions.

What you seeFirst method to try
An inner function and its derivativeReverse chain rule or a direct substitution
A product such as \(x\cos(2x)\)Parts, because differentiating the polynomial lowers its degree
A square such as \(\sin^2x\)Use a double-angle identity before integrating
A rational function with a factorable denominatorCheck for \(\frac{f'}{f}\); otherwise try partial fractions
A supplied change of variableSubstitute every factor and convert both limits

blocks.html: Substitute the lower limit into every term of a primitive. For example, a cosine term can survive at zero.

blocks.title: Evaluate both boundary values

retry.feedback: At the lower limit the primitive equals \(\frac14\), which must also be subtracted.

blocks.hint: Use parts with \(v=\frac12\sin(2x)\) and evaluate the complete primitive at both endpoints.
blocks.solution: \[\left[\frac{x\sin(2x)}2+\frac{\cos(2x)}4\right]_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}}=-\frac14-\frac14=-\frac12.\]

sections.title: How can the endpoints simplify a by-parts calculation?
sections.label: Check the boundary term
sections.intro: The product term at the endpoints and the remaining integral may behave differently.

blocks.html: Write both evaluations and look for zeros before simplifying. The remainder can survive even if the endpoint product vanishes.

blocks.html: When a minus sign is outside a bracket, subtract the complete lower-endpoint expression.

blocks.title: Apply integration by parts and keep the remainder
blocks.hint: Choose the factor that becomes simpler on differentiation. Subtract the entire remainder.
blocks.solution:
Choose \(u=x,\quad \frac{\mathrm dv}{\mathrm dx}=\sin{\left(6 x \right)}\). Then \(\frac{\mathrm du}{\mathrm dx}=1,\quad v=- \frac{\cos{\left(6 x \right)}}{6}\).

Write the product term, then subtract the integral of \(- \frac{\cos{\left(6 x \right)}}{6}\).

Integrating that remainder gives \(- \frac{x \cos{\left(6 x \right)}}{6} + \frac{\sin{\left(6 x \right)}}{36}+C\) for the original primitive.

Evaluate the primitive at the upper limit, then subtract its value at the lower limit. The integral is \(- \frac{\pi}{18}\).

examples.title: Reduce a linear factor to a constant
examples.question: Find \(\int (2x+1)e^{2x}\,dx\).
solution: \[\int (2x+1)e^{2x}\,dx=\left(x+\frac12\right)e^{2x}-\int e^{2x}\,dx.\]
The remaining primitive is \(\frac12e^{2x}\). The terms cancel to give \(xe^{2x}+C\). Differentiating returns \((2x+1)e^{2x}\).

examples.title: Reveal the rational remainder
examples.question: Find \(\int \ln(3x+1)\,dx\), for \(x>-\frac13\).
solution: Use \(u=\ln(3x+1)\) and \(v'=1\). This gives \(u'=\frac{3}{3x+1}\) and \(v=x\).
\[\int\ln(3x+1)\,dx=x\ln(3x+1)-\int\left(1-\frac{1}{3x+1}\right)\,dx.\]
Integrate the split remainder and collect logarithms. The result is \(\left(x+\frac13\right)\ln(3x+1)-x+C\).

examples.title: Lower a quadratic factor twice
examples.question: Find \(\int x^2e^{-x}\,dx\).
solution:
Use parts with \(u=x^2,\ v=-e^{-x}\).

\[\int x^2e^{-x}\,dx=-x^2e^{-x}+\int 2xe^{-x}\,dx.\]

StepDifferentiated factorPrimitive used
First\(u=x^2\)\(v=-e^{-x}\)
Second\(u=2x\)\(v=-e^{-x}\)

For the new integral, use \(u=2x\) and the same primitive \(v=-e^{-x}\). It gives \(-2xe^{-x}-2e^{-x}\), up to a constant.
Collect terms to obtain \(-(x^2+2x+2)e^{-x}+C\).

examples.title: Evaluate a trigonometric product
examples.question: Find \(\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}}x\sin(2x)\,dx\), using radians.
solution: Select \(u=x\), \(v'=\sin(2x)\). Then \(u'=1\) and \(v=-\frac12\cos(2x)\).
\[\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}}x\sin(2x)\,dx=\left[-\frac{x\cos(2x)}2+\frac{\sin(2x)}4\right]_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}}.\]
At the upper limit, \(\cos\pi=-1\) and \(\sin\pi=0\). The lower value is \(0\), so the integral is \(\frac{\pi}{4}\).

examples.title: Apply integration by parts and keep the remainder
examples.question: Write \(\int \left(2 x + 3\right) \mathrm e^{7 x}\,\mathrm dx\) as \((Ax+B)\mathrm e^{7 x}+C\). Find \(A\) and \(B\).
solution: Choose \(u=2 x + 3,\quad \frac{\mathrm dv}{\mathrm dx}=\mathrm e^{7 x}\). Then \(\frac{\mathrm du}{\mathrm dx}=2,\quad v=\frac{\mathrm e^{7 x}}{7}\).
Write the product term, then subtract the integral of \(\frac{2 \mathrm e^{7 x}}{7}\).
Integrating that remainder gives \(\frac{\left(14 x + 19\right) \mathrm e^{7 x}}{49}+C\) for the original primitive.

examples.title: Apply integration by parts and keep the remainder
examples.question: Write \(\int 4 \ln{\left(x \right)}\,\mathrm dx\) as \(Ax\ln x+Bx+C\) for \(x>0\). Find \(A\) and \(B\).
solution: Choose \(u=\ln{\left(x \right)},\quad \frac{\mathrm dv}{\mathrm dx}=4\). Then \(\frac{\mathrm du}{\mathrm dx}=\frac{1}{x},\quad v=4 x\).
Write the product term, then subtract the integral of \(4\).
Integrating that remainder gives \(4 x \left(\ln{\left(x \right)} - 1\right)+C\) for the original primitive.

examples.title: Apply integration by parts and keep the remainder
examples.question: Evaluate \(\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}x \sin{\left(4 x \right)}\,\mathrm dx\) exactly by parts.
solution: Choose \(u=x,\quad \frac{\mathrm dv}{\mathrm dx}=\sin{\left(4 x \right)}\). Then \(\frac{\mathrm du}{\mathrm dx}=1,\quad v=- \frac{\cos{\left(4 x \right)}}{4}\).
Write the product term, then subtract the integral of \(- \frac{\cos{\left(4 x \right)}}{4}\).
Integrating that remainder gives \(- \frac{x \cos{\left(4 x \right)}}{4} + \frac{\sin{\left(4 x \right)}}{16}+C\) for the original primitive.
Evaluate the primitive at the upper limit, then subtract its value at the lower limit. The integral is \(- \frac{\pi}{8}\).

glossary.definition: A function whose derivative gives the original integrand.
The evaluated product \([uv]_a^b\) in a definite application of integration by parts.
The total with regions below the horizontal axis contributing a negative value.

revision.body: Reverse the product rule: \(\int uv'\,dx=uv-\int u'v\,dx\). Pick \(u\) to simplify by differentiation and \(v'\) to give an easy primitive.

extraPractice.title: Apply integration by parts and keep the remainder
extraPractice.prompt: Write \(\int \left(5 x + 1\right) \mathrm e^{3 x}\,\mathrm dx\) as \((Ax+B)\mathrm e^{3 x}+C\). Find \(A\) and \(B\).
extraPractice.hint: Choose the factor that becomes simpler on differentiation. Subtract the entire remainder.
extraPractice.solution:
Choose \(u=5 x + 1,\quad \frac{\mathrm dv}{\mathrm dx}=\mathrm e^{3 x}\). Then \(\frac{\mathrm du}{\mathrm dx}=5,\quad v=\frac{\mathrm e^{3 x}}{3}\).

Write the product term, then subtract the integral of \(\frac{5 \mathrm e^{3 x}}{3}\).

Integrating that remainder gives \(\frac{\left(15 x - 2\right) \mathrm e^{3 x}}{9}+C\) for the original primitive.

Write the product term, then subtract the integral of \(7\).

extraPractice.title: Apply integration by parts and keep the remainder
extraPractice.hint: Choose the factor that becomes simpler on differentiation. Subtract the entire remainder.
extraPractice.solution:
Choose \(u=x,\quad \frac{\mathrm dv}{\mathrm dx}=\cos{\left(3 x \right)}\). Then \(\frac{\mathrm du}{\mathrm dx}=1,\quad v=\frac{\sin{\left(3 x \right)}}{3}\).

Evaluate the primitive at the upper limit, then subtract its value at the lower limit. The integral is \(- \frac{2}{9}\).

extraPractice.title: Apply integration by parts and keep the remainder
extraPractice.prompt: Write \(\int \left(3 x - 2\right) \mathrm e^{- 2 x}\,\mathrm dx\) as \((Ax+B)\mathrm e^{- 2 x}+C\). Find \(A\) and \(B\).

Write the product term, then subtract the integral of \(- \frac{3 \mathrm e^{- 2 x}}{2}\).

Integrating that remainder gives \(\frac{\left(1 - 6 x\right) \mathrm e^{- 2 x}}{4}+C\) for the original primitive.

extraPractice.hint: Choose the factor that becomes simpler on differentiation. Subtract the entire remainder.

extraPractice.title: Apply integration by parts and keep the remainder
extraPractice.prompt: Evaluate \(\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}2 x \sin{\left(2 x \right)}\,\mathrm dx\) exactly by parts.
extraPractice.hint: Choose the factor that becomes simpler on differentiation. Subtract the entire remainder.
extraPractice.solution:
Choose \(u=2 x,\quad \frac{\mathrm dv}{\mathrm dx}=\sin{\left(2 x \right)}\). Then \(\frac{\mathrm du}{\mathrm dx}=2,\quad v=- \frac{\cos{\left(2 x \right)}}{2}\).

Write the product term, then subtract the integral of \(- \cos{\left(2 x \right)}\).

Integrating that remainder gives \(- x \cos{\left(2 x \right)} + \frac{\sin{\left(2 x \right)}}{2}+C\) for the original primitive.

Evaluate the primitive at the upper limit, then subtract its value at the lower limit. The integral is \(\frac{\pi}{2}\).
